title: Feedback Without Losing Confidence
script: Host: [welcoming] A tutor returns your essay covered in comments. Your first thought is, “I am not good enough for this course.” What should happen next?
Guest: First, separate the work from the person. The comments describe this draft, not my permanent ability or worth.
Host: Easy to say, but difficult when the mark is disappointing.

Guest: [honestly] I agree. I give myself time to feel disappointed, then I sort the feedback into categories: argument, evidence, structure, and language. A page of comments becomes a smaller set of skills.
Host: What if some advice is unclear?
Guest: I prepare a specific question. Instead of asking, “Why is this bad?” I ask, “Could you show me where the connection between these two paragraphs becomes unclear?”
Host: [curious] Should students follow every comment without question?
Guest: They should understand the reason behind it. If two tutors suggest different approaches, the student can ask about the assignment criteria and make an informed choice.
Host: How do you protect confidence while still accepting criticism?
Guest: By using evidence. I compare drafts, keep examples of improvements, and notice which problems no longer appear. Confidence grows more reliably from progress than from praise alone.
Host: What role can classmates play?
Guest: A useful peer describes their reading experience: “I expected evidence here,” or “This example changed my understanding.” They should not take over the writing.
Host: [reflective] And when feedback feels harsh?
Guest: Focus first on any usable information. If the language is disrespectful or the marking seems inconsistent, raise the concern through the proper academic process and keep the original record.
Host: Give us one final rule.
Guest: Turn feedback into one next action. Revision becomes manageable when “improve everything” changes into “rewrite the claim and add one reliable source.”
